rachel_kneebone.name: Rachel Kneebone
rachel_kneebone.web_blurb:
Rachel Kneebone's work addresses and questions the human condition: renewal, life cycles and the physical body. Working primarily in sculpture that embraces the unpredictable nature of its medium – porcelain - Kneebone focuses on ideas of movement and metamorphosis, transformation and suspension and the material manifestation of fluid physical states. Kneebone has stated that her work is 'concerned with inhabiting the body, what it is to be alive in the world'.

Born 1973 in Oxfordshire, UK; lives and works in London, UK.

shigeyuki_tamba.name: Shigeyuki Tamba
shigeyuki_tamba.web_blurb:
Shigeyuki Tamba carves shapes out of white porcelain, using flowers and other plants as his subject.

Born 1978 in Sapporo, Hokkaido Japan; lives and works in Sapporo.

hitomi_hosono.name: Hitomi Hosono
hitomi_hosono.web_blurb:
Hitomi Hosono’s detailed porcelain vessels reference the natural world and botanical specimens. Her signature style is inspired by Wedgwood Jasperware and consists of creating original sprig models and plaster moulds based on botanical examples which she then applies in layers onto a pottery base.
A large piece takes around 1 year and 6 months for the whole process. A half year to develop new sprig design and the mould, about one month to complete the porcelain piece itself and about 10-12 months to dry slowly. A small piece takes approximately 4 months to complete, dry, fire and gild.
With a chalk-like finish and gold embellishments, the work captivates with its delicacy and has attracted the patronage of curators from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum.

Born 1978 in Gifu Prefecture, Japan; lives and works in London, UK.

bridget_macklin.name: Bridget Macklin
bridget_macklin.web_blurb:
Bridget Macklin’s work demonstrates her desire to tell the story of our landscape and the way that we relate to it: the behaviours of man during the geological epoch now known as the Anthropocene. She is interested in the simplicity of form, creating experimental work, and often using unglazed clay. Her works are made from pure porcelain to which she adds found materials and images. She delights in experimenting and in taking risks, striving for ever thinner work which only reveals its full nature on closer inspection.

Lives and works in Cornwall, UK.

tamsyn_trevorrow.name: Tamsyn Trevorrow
tamsyn_trevorrow.web_blurb:
Tamsyn Trevorrow’s work explores the material effects of time on the natural world, in particular the interaction between land and sea and the ever changing landscape of these liminal spaces. She uses colour, form and texture to transmute the temporal into experience. The beautiful and rugged landscape surrounded by coastline of Cornwall, as well as the Cornish mines, mine deposits and boat/shipwrecks, all offer a rich source of inspiration. Their structures and weathered and corroded textures are reflected in the construction of her clay forms.
Her pieces are mainly built by hand with a heavily grogged local stoneware clay. Each piece is then usually cut, reshaped and sculpted; adding and removing sections as the piece evolves. This results in a spontaneous and instinctive sculpture, which invites the eye to explore from all angles, in, around and through.
The colours are a result of using a variety of different slips (some from local river beds) and glazes that she makes herself. Her Work is often multi-fired over a range of temperatures building up the textures or colours.

Born in St Ives, Cornwall UK; lives and works in St Ives.

helene_kirchmair.name: Helene Kirchmair
helene_kirchmair.web_blurb:
Helene Kirchmair’s work is often based on using and alienating already existing, industrially manufactured products. A trivial objet trouvè is transformed by a location change and material-transformation to an individual object and unique ceramic piece.
The viewer is referred to the triviality. It’s playing with being and appearance. With sense and nonsense. Kirchmair integrates wire, plastic, paint, plaster, concrete, as well as ready mades with ceramics, which always remains the predominant and preferred material. Often graphic works - drawings, photographs or etchings - complete her ceramic objects.

Born 1981 in Hall, Tirol Austria; lives and works in Austria.

diane_griffin.name: Diane Griffin
diane_griffin.web_blurb:
Diane Griffin’s ceramic sculptures are inspired by our human experience, and how we connect with each other and the world around us through rituals and ceremonies. She first became interested in our use of rituals during a trip to the Wailing Wall in Jerusalem in 1985, watching in fascination as people prayed and left messages as a way to feel a sense of connection to each other, their spiritual selves and a higher power.
Her poetic sculptures are rich in contrasting textures. Rough and cracked surfaces are united with delicate sheets of ruffled porcelain. Precious metallic elements further accentuate the organic textures, a glint of something precious in amongst earthy textures.
Griffin enjoys using a variety of techniques and clays in combination. Throwing, hand building and carving are used to achieve different textures, surfaces and forms. She uses layers of slips and glazes that are fired many times to achieve the required result. She works in porcelain and earthenware clays with a variety of processes, each with its own rhythm and nuance which are united into the final piece.

Born in London, UK; lives and works in Northamptonshire, UK.

aram_rios.name: Aram Rios
aram_rios.web_blurb:
Aram Ríos’ work is characterised by mixed-media experimentation, with a focus on ceramics. He leads an experimental ceramics workshop for people with functional diversity while actively producing his own artistic work.

Born 1990 in Vigo, Spain, lives and works in Vigo.

tomomi_tanaka.name: Tomomi Tanaka
tomomi_tanaka.web_blurb:
Tomomi Tanaka’s works consist of many lamellas of clay which are attached to the surface of a hand-built clay core. She sees the layers of lamella as mirroring the suppressed feelings piled up in her mind. Her process starts with a simple sketch that aims to express the swirling of emotions she feels inside her body. This is then transformed into a three-dimensional piece, starting with the core.
Initially the core of Tanaka’s pieces was a simple sphere, and her focus was on the process of attaching and layering, not on the final form. Over time, her work has evolved to include forms with beautiful curved lines, like undulating waves, enveloped by layers of lamella. In some works the core is pulled or constricted to create the forms akin to limbs or waists, and the shape of the lamellas is more varied.
Tanaka’s pieces seem flowing and alive, defying the solidity of the medium. While her pieces are often described by analogy to natural phenomena such as waves or living creatures, she considers them an expression of her internal world and hopes they can evoke the same feelings in the viewer that drove her to create them.

Born 1983 in Hyogo, Japan.

leonie_rutter.name: Leonie Rutter
leonie_rutter.web_blurb:
A mechanical engineer by profession, Leonie Rutter was introduced to clay at evening classes, over 30 years ago. She has been exploring wheel thrown and hand building techniques ever since.
Her ceramics are characterised by their flowing lines and minimalist, contemporary designs. With a focus on form and texture, she aims to create beautifully tactile pieces that convey a sense of balance and harmony. Her hand thrown porcelain vessels are inlaid with patterns of coloured porcelain whilst the abstract sculptural forms are hand built from stoneware clay and have a beautifully textured surface.
Rutter’s engineering background adds a unique perspective to her ceramic works, allowing her to push the boundaries of the medium whilst creating forms which are visually appealing. Her deliberate use of asymmetry adds a complexity to the designs, which invites the viewer to explore the pieces from every angle.

Lives and works near Kirkby Lonsdale, UK.

cecil_kemperink.name: Cecil Kemperink
cecil_kemperink.web_blurb:
Cecil Kemperinks’s sculptures are connections between her varied passions: textile, clay, dance, fashion and sculpture. They are constructed from rings of clay, which symbolise connection. Every ring is essential and influences every other.
Kemperink works intuitively; the sculpture grows in her hands. The manual process of connecting the many linked circles of clay gives rise to an attentive, and labour-intensive process. Her sculptures are dynamic and multisensory experiences: Touching the work causes the rings to shift against each other, letting the viewer reshape the work, hear the sound, and experience the tactile qualities of the clay.

Born 1963 in Almelo, Netherlands; lives and works on Texel, Netherlands

anne_sophie_boulogne.name: Anne Sophie Boulogne
anne_sophie_boulogne.web_blurb:
Anne Sophie Boulogne’s work initially focused on grogged clay and raku, creating pieces with an ethnic flair. However, viewing ceramics as an infinitely liberating space, her desire to constantly experiment and push the boundaries imposed by the medium led her to porcelain—a demanding material that allows for exquisite delicacy.
The sculptures she creates are inspired by the fascinating and magical universe of the Abyss. It’s an unknown and mysterious world where even the richest imagination can still be surprised. The often geometric and always harmonious forms resonate with boundless freedom and represent, to her, the perfect embodiment of beauty in nature.

Lives and works in Saint-Brès, France.

shinhye_you.name: Shinhye You
shinhye_you.web_blurb:
Shinhye You constructs fiction that follows the principles of magical realism and translates them into visual forms. The pieces become evidence of a written story, allowing the allegorical figures to become alive in our world. Intertwined between the allegory and the existing world, Shinhye's artworks vitalize stories and initiate conversations with the readers and the figures. Shinhye believes clay and its transformation into ceramics have similarities in creating a fictional world with visible words. Through the ceramics that are depicted in the stories, the magic within once again gains life.
Shinhye creates ceramics by assembling small units of raw clay which she believes is a traditional technique that requires effort and skill. The units manifest human desires and emotions and the base of the sculptures are abstract forms that symbolise the figures in her stories.
The story depicts a fictional world where every person bequeaths small crystals after death. The relics, left as an essence of one's life, grow and linger in the living world and become a memorial to a person who once existed. As the stones grow, their form slowly shapes into a form that symbolises the life of the owners. People can speculate about the life of the owners through the form and the behaviour of the organs attached to the surface of the stones.

Born 1992 in South Korea; lives and works in London, UK.

tim_fluck.name: Tim Fluck
tim_fluck.web_blurb:
Tim Fluck primarily works with slip cast porcelain forms. His process includes 3D printing (to create the moulds) and resin casting for transparent pieces.
Conceptually his work explores the notion of utopia as a process (rather than a solution,) in which the promise of an ideal is never realised but remains on an endless loop of desire. His work brings together seemingly disparate forms and textures, from Minimalist-inspired Brutalism to the Maximalism of Memphis Design. The contrast of clean and seemingly infinite forms, with playful and colourful imperfect protrusions, convey a precarious harmony and comment on a perpetual reach for the elusive promise of utopia.

silke_wellmeier.name: Silke Wellmeier
silke_wellmeier.web_blurb:
Silke Wellmeier works with Limoges porcelain, freely assembling it by hand into thin-walled objects/vessels with an almost organic-looking surface. She usually works in series on a particular theme, re-shaping, reproducing and documenting.
In her series “protected spaces” each piece reproduces the outline of a different nature conservation area in porcelain, enveloping the interior in a delicate but strong wall, as if protecting it from the outside.

Lives and works in Tecklenburg, Germany.

yuta_segawa.name: Yuta Segawa
yuta_segawa.web_blurb:
Yuta Segawa specialises in producing miniature pottery. He learned ceramic skills in Japan and China and developed these into the techniques of his miniature pots in London. All his miniature pots are thrown individually by hand, using special wheels and tools to work at minute scales. He uses more than five hundred custom-made glazes to finish the works.
Miniature pottery relates to the issue of the relationship between artists’ bodies and their works. It is a challenge to test the limits of what a human body can achieve on such a small scale.

Born 1988 in Shizuoka, Japan; lives and works in London, UK.

valerie_bernardini.name: Valerie Bernardini
valerie_bernardini.web_blurb:
Valerie Bernardini works with black or white porcelain and glass. She likes the contrast between the strength of the material and its apparent fragility. Her work consists of cast, extruded and constructed forms that are born from stress, pressure and tension. Bernardini is fascinated by the contrast of supple movement turning hard and brittle, and tries to capture this sense of “frozen movement” in her pieces, perhaps inspired by her background in photography.
Her recent works are created by slip casting, using complex segmented moulds that are stacked in layers. The design of these moulds starts from an irregular outline, which is rotated to create offset profiles at each layer. The pieces are cast in one piece and fired multiple times, using glass granules to create intricate surface textures.

Born 1968 in Brittany, France; lives and/ works in London, UK.

clare_palmer.name: Clare Palmer
clare_palmer.web_blurb:
Clare Palmer’s work is rooted in the personal, representing themes of emotional impact – from upheaval to trauma. Unusually for a maker, her sketchbooks consist primarily of words. Her process begins with a written exploration of an emotional experience or state of mind. Whilst doing this she gets a strong visual impression of the direction a piece will take, which is then captured as a sketch and one or two-word working title. With these, the work in clay begins.
She crafts her one-off sculptures and vessels in a variety of stoneware and porcelain clays, using both throwing and handbuilding techniques. The handbuilt sculptures are constructed directly on the kiln-shelves, using textured slabs: shaping, tearing, joining and lastly propping thoroughly to prevent unwanted warping in the kiln. After initial firing, oxides are layered up, before glazing with a selection of glazes, to create subtle variations of colour and tone - with occasional dark accents - to reflect the narratives explored through the work.
Her vessels start life as thrown forms which she makes on the wheel, before cutting, joining and distorting. Oxides and engobes are used sparingly to enhance details, before glazing with a quiet palette of glazes. ​

Lives and works in London, UK.

moniek_van_der_kroef.name: Moniek van der Kroef
moniek_van_der_kroef.web_blurb:
Moniek van der Kroef works in multiple media, including painting and poetry. Recently she prefers ceramics, attracted by clay's history and timelessness. She combines wheel-thrown works with molds and hand-building techniques, modifying her pieces on the fly to infuse them with a sense of life. ​

Lives and works in Amsterdam, Netherlands.

rose_schmits.name: Rose Schmits
rose_schmits.web_blurb:
Born and raised in the historic city of Delft in the Netherlands, Rose Schmits is a London based ceramicist whose art is inspired by her experiences as a trans woman and the rich pottery tradition of her city of origin. She is best known for her role as studio technician on the Channel 4 show The Great Pottery Throw Down since series 4.
One of her more prominent series of works, the Crawler Pots collection, involves porcelain vessels seemingly having sprouted spidery legs and tendrils ready to scuttle away. The lively vessels speak of bodies, transformation, sex, gender, monstrousness, and beauty, as well as exploring unexpected approaches to ceramic practice. Their fragile porcelain tendrils and legs demand these objects are treated with respect and their autonomy as objects acknowledged.
Schmits’ work is both fine art and craft, and a statement that the rules of pottery can always be broken in new and interesting ways.

Lives and works in London, UK.

josefina_isaza.name: Josefina Isaza
josefina_isaza.web_blurb:
Josefina Isaza gained her BFA in crafts from The University Of The Arts, Philadelphia under the guidance of world-renowned potter, James Makins. She continued at Uarts as an artist-in-residence, and then travelled to Tokoname, Japan for a further residency at Kyouei-Gamma!. Josefina had the fortune to be taught by many ceramic masters, allowing her to embody the freedom, and spontaneity she observed in their practice.
She continues to develop her own style largely influenced by Japanese contemporary aesthetics, concepts of imperfect beauty, and close observation of nature. She describes herself as highly conscious of the spatial environment in relation to the material, and immerses herself in its meditative qualities. This is conveyed in the meticulous application of hundreds of individual elements to her pieces. She creates highly visual and tactile surfaces, informed by a love for nature and fine detail.
Her work is intended to provoke multiple sensory modalities, and thus spark a curiosity in the viewer. It demonstrates how visual stimuli can be achieved by grouping single elements to form a larger gestalt whole, as reflected throughout nature.

Born in Colombia, lives and works in London, UK.

anna_smyth.name: Anna Smyth
anna_smyth.web_blurb:
Anna uses porcelain, a pure and sensitive material, to express inner responses to observations and experiences: as another voice speaking in a visual, three dimensional language. Her recent work includes crystalline glazes, which spontaneously form intricate structures during the firing process. She develops her own glaze recipes and firing curves, constantly refining the process.

Lives and works in County Down, Northern Ireland, UK.

penny_little.name: Penny Little
penny_little.web_blurb:
Since the first time she held a piece of cold smooth porcelain clay in her hands Penny Little felt an affinity with this wonderful translucent material. She loves working with porcelain, a beautiful clay that needs to be handled with a mixture of confidence and softness. Because she hand-builds, a long, drawn-out process, she never quite knows what the final form of her pieces will be.
She is a passionate advocate for hand-made work and finds a connection whenever someone picks up one of her pieces – as if, just for a second, her hand goes into theirs.
Penny uses gold and platinum lustre, filling her work with light at the final stage. This comes after a long process of hand-forming, carving, finishing, firing, glazing, firing again and then adding the lustre in the third and final firing. The contrast of the smooth luxurious lustre interior and the organic non-glazed exterior which leaves the porcelain to speak for itself, gives her pieces a very tactile quality.

adrian_bates.name: Adrian Bates
adrian_bates.web_blurb:
Adrian Bates was drawn from an early age to calligraphic forms – particularly how the outer and inner curves of letterforms relate to, and interact with each other to give grace to the overall figure. He sees similar relationships everywhere, and his ceramics carry this interest forward. The walls of his vessels – defining inner and outer space – correlate to the body of letterforms – and the serif-like way in which many of them terminate at lip or spout.
He is also influenced by primal forms contained inside other 'vessels' – human, plant and animal – all containing life and defined by their interaction with nature. In these ways his work connects, not so much with a place, as a culture – our relationships with nature and each other…

Lives and works in Gloucestershire, UK

masamichi_yoshikawa.name: Masamichi Yoshikawa
masamichi_yoshikawa.web_blurb:
Masamichi Yoshikawa specialises in sculptural forms covered with a pale blue seihakuji glaze. His works are assembled from slabs of clay that are carved into imperfect geometric forms and covered with a gloopy, dripping glaze. Hidden on the underside of some of them are calligraphic designs drawn in a darker, cobalt blue.
He graduated from the Nippon Designer Institute in 1968, and moved to Tokoname, a city renowned for its ceramic production since the 12th century. His works have won numerous awards, and are featured in museums worldwide.

Born in Chigasaki, Japan in 1946; lives and works in Tokoname, Japan.

miki_tomii.name: Miki Tomii
miki_tomii.web_blurb:
Miki Tomii combines ceramics and glass to form intriguing sculptural objects. The materials combine and transform in the kiln, creating intricate textures at the interface. Her work is inspired both by the properties of the materials, and by her own experiences, especially of nature. She tries to represent the “energy of decay” she feels from the traces of previous life in the clay.
Miki studied at Akita University and Tokyo University of Fine Arts and Music, earning a Masters in Glass Art in 2022.

Born in Yamagata, Japan in 1997; lives and works in Seto, Japan.

kim_colebrook.name: Kim Colebrook
kim_colebrook.web_blurb:
Kim Colebrook incorporates texture and narrative into her practice. Her works are handbuilt or cast, consisting of simple forms consisting of nerikomi blocks, which combine black and white clay in layers mirroring geological formations. She is inspired by the history, geology, and people of South Wales, with a current focus on the South Wales Coalfield.

Lives and works in Abergavenny, UK.

kouzo_takeuchi.name: Kouzo Takeuchi
kouzo_takeuchi.web_blurb:
Kouzo Takeuchi’s “Modern Remains” series is inspired by his fascination with aggregations of geometric shapes, and their connection to ancient ruined architecture. His distinctive broken and fragmented forms are the product of a serendipitous accident, when he dropped a prototype piece and found the results more beautiful than before.
His works are assembled from slip-cast pieces of square tubing that he then breaks with a hammer, trying to achieve a balance between the precise original shapes and the randomness of the rough, broken surfaces.

Born in 1977 in Kato, Japan; lives and works in Kato, Japan

yoichiro_kamei.name: Yoichiro Kamei
yoichiro_kamei.web_blurb:
Yoichiro Kamei’s “Lattice Receptacle” series is based on assembling a simple repeating unit – a small cube with pierced sides – into larger lattices. The individual cubes are slip-cast and glazed together, creating a subtle roundness at interior corners where the cubes meet. His designs play with light and shadow, and suggest to the viewer that they could extend to tile space infinitely.

Born in 1974 in Kagawa Prefecture, Japan; lives and works in Nishihara, Japan

darren_emenau.name: Darren Emenau
darren_emenau.web_blurb:
Darren Emenau is inspired by the rugged coastline and landscape of his native New Brunswick. His works, with their flocked or cracked textures, bring to mind moss covered rocks, lichen, or bark. He is a prolific experimenter, gathering wild clays, developing glazes, and coming up with new surface treatments. He does not shy away from using non-standard techniques, including acrylic paints and applying electrostatic flocking after the firing.

Born in New Brunswick, Canada; lives and works in Canada.

ebony_russell.name: Ebony Russell
ebony_russell.web_blurb:
Ebony Russell uses a unique technique, mixing porcelain clay to a soft consistency and then applying it with a piping bag. She initially used piped clay as decoration on top of traditional solid forms, but then discovered that, using porcelain, it could be used to build delicate, free-standing shapes. She builds her works in layers, slowly enough that they are almost dry when the last layer is placed. They appear intricate and playful, seeming as if they were made from piled-up cake icing, with squiggly lines and perforations.
Her motifs include vessel-like forms and architectural elements such as columns, and are decorated with flowers, garlands, and ribbons. She draws inspiration from her childhood memories, of her grandmother's china collection, a magazine of birthday cake recipes, and all the pretty things of her memories.

Born in Melbourne, Australia; lives and works in New South Wales, Australia.

myung_nam_an.name: Myung Nam An
myung_nam_an.web_blurb:
Myung Nam An’s work is inspired by the material properties and limitations of the porcelain she uses. Her process start with a human form, such as the eye, based on which she develops hundreds of variations, exploring shapes, decorations, and colour. Many of her pieces consist of intricate assemblies of hundreds of tiny spikes, tendrils, or bumps.

Born in Seoul, South Korea; lives and works in London, UK.

raquel_eidem.name: Raquel Eidem
raquel_eidem.web_blurb:
Raquel Eidem’s work is based on social and political criticism. She combines a conceptual approach to art with a strong sense of aesthetic balance. Her “industrial common” series engages with the transition from artisanal production and figurative art to industrial production and the rise of abstraction.

Born in Spain; lives and works in Seville, Spain.

ain_choi.name: Ain Choi
ain_choi.web_blurb: Ain Choi’s work is inspired by waves, a fundamental concept in physics that appears in many phenomena from fundamental quantum field theory and relativity to sound and the surface of the ocean. Her works are built from layers, starting with a cylindrical shape and stacking multiple distorted versions of it on top of each other. On close inspection the surface reveals a complex three-dimensional pattern in the matte glaze, reminiscent of earth. She considers them “waves moving through the soil”.

saeri_seo.name: Saeri Seo
saeri_seo.web_blurb:
Saeri Seo’s work is inspired by her struggles with “good child syndrome”, the consequence of the constant pressure to be perfect in both behaviour and achievements imposed on children. Her pieces start out in the form of traditional wheel-thrown Korean pottery, but are broken by the literal pressure imposed on them. From these shattered pieces new life blooms, in the form of delicate hand formed flowers that grow within and around them.

Born in South Korea, lives and works in the UK.

valerie_mclean.name: Valerie Mclean
valerie_mclean.web_blurb:
Valerie Mclean’s work is inspired by the Mediterranean landscapes of her childhood in France. Their stone villages, crumbling castles, medieval churches, and archaeological sites are not directly represented, but they shine through in the muted, earthen colours and complex surface textures of her works. She achieves these without glazes and with a single firing. Some of the decorations seem like writing in some unknown language hinting at a history we can only imagine.
Her “Fragments” series initially consisted of small ceramic pieces suspended in a welded steel frame. Serendipitously, she found that the holes intended for mounting the pieces on the frame also added interest on their own, evoking windows.

Born in France, lives and works in the UK.

soyeon_gim.name: Soyeon Gim
soyeon_gim.web_blurb:
Soyeon Gim’s work explores the potential of materials with a personal and figurative language. Her pieces are assemblages of simple shapes (wheel thrown or hand carved) with a wide range of surface textures and glazes. The resulting pieces have a sense of playfulness about them, sometimes seeming precariously balanced, like a child's block tower about to collapse. Soyeon documents her pieces meticulously on her website, an “Archive of Forms” with by now over 180 unique pieces.

Born in South Korea, lives and works in Seoul, South Korea.

micaela_schoop.name: Micaela Schoop
micaela_schoop.web_blurb:
Micaela Schoop’s work fuses abstract shapes, which she sees as more universally and intuitively understood, with elaborate patterns of underglaze decoration based on cultural traditions from around the world. Through these patterns, which come from both pottery traditions but also architecture and textiles, she explores cultural identity, the common and the unique.
Beyond the visual, the tactile sensation of handling her pieces is an important part of their appeal. This is especially true of the “Handschmeichler” (hand-pleaser) series, whose size and rounded shapes almost demand to be picked up and explored.

Born in Germany, lives and works in the UK.

erum_aamir.name: Erum Aamir
erum_aamir.web_blurb:
Erum Aamir’s background in physics led her to look to science for inspiration for her work. She is especially fascinated by the hidden, microscopic, world all around us, such as the complexity hidden in a single grain of pollen. Her works are not direct copies of nature, but they blur the line between imagination and reality.
She creates intricate pieces made of many small, thin, porcelain elements made entirely by hand. They are not designed ahead of time, but rather grow organically as the piece is slowly assembled in a repetitive, meditative process.

Born in Pakistan, lives and works in Manchester, UK.

yimou_huang.name: Yimou Huang
yimou_huang.web_blurb:
Yimou Huang is a UK-based sculptor whose practice explores the Taoist principle of Wu Wei—action through inaction—translated into quietly dynamic ceramic forms that sit between control and spontaneity. Currently undertaking a practice-based PhD at the University of Dundee, Huang draws on Chinese Taoist thought and Western eco-feminist theory to question human relationships with nature and power. His work has gained growing international recognition, including selection for the British Ceramics Biennial’s FRESH exhibition, where his subtly textured surfaces and fragmented bodily motifs evoke vulnerability, resilience, and the fragile balance of contemporary life.

Born in China, lives and works in the UK.

alison_rees.name: Alison Rees
alison_rees.web_blurb:
Alison Rees’s work translates walking, mapping and memory into delicate compositions of porcelain “pages.” With a background in archaeology and a PhD in ceramics from the Royal College of Art, she explores how layers of history, place and everyday experience can be abstracted into grids and sequences of individually made clay sheets. Her wall-based installations and postcard-like pieces invite viewers to read landscape and self as a quiet, unfolding narrative in clay.​

Born 1970 in the UK, lives and works in London, UK.

jenny_thomas.name: Jenny Thomas
jenny_thomas.web_blurb:
Jenny Thomas’s practice is rooted in the quiet necessity of making. What began as a search for calm within the chaos of PTSD and anxiety became a tactile language – one that allows her to speak through material where words fall short. She is drawn to natural imperfection: irregular forms, subtle shifts, marks left by the hand. These elements – fragile yet intentional – reflect a tension she often carries between control and release.
Her work captures movement held in pause – a sweep of gesture, a breath caught in porcelain. Embracing translucency, suspended forms and layered surfaces, Jenny explores contrast not as opposition, but as balance: strength within softness, chaos within calm.

Lives and works in the UK.

caroline_gray.name: Caroline Gray
caroline_gray.web_blurb:
Caroline Gray’s sculptural vessels and wall pieces explore the emotional charge of colour, shadow and architectural form. Initially trained as a textile designer with a career in trend forecasting before completing an MA in Fine Art at Chelsea College of Art, she came to clay in 2018 and quickly established a distinctive practice. Selected as one of 25 leading emerging artists for FRESH 2023 at the British Ceramics Biennial, where she received a residency award, Gray creates thoughtful, abstract compositions that sit between design and fine art, inviting quiet, contemplative engagement

Lives and works in London, UK.

inaba_chikako.name: Inaba Chikako
inaba_chikako.web_blurb:
Inaba Chikako’s sculptural stoneware vessels echo the fragile curves of withering leaves and other botanical forms. Working largely in creamy white glazes, she hand-builds intricately veined pieces that appear both delicate and resilient, evoking stillness, impermanence, and the quiet transformation found in nature.

Born 1974 in Yokohama, Japan, lives and works in Japan.

sazan.name: Sazan (Hiroki Shinkawa)
sazan.orig_name: 砂山 (さざん) / 新川宏樹
sazan.web_blurb:
Sazan’s works are finely detailed, their hand-painted surfaces blending traditional Kutani and Imari-inspired motifs with a crisp, modern sensibility. Working on carefully thrown porcelain forms, he layers luminous enamels and gold overglaze to create intricate patterning that hovers between decorative design and narrative illustration. His work is prized for its precise line, saturated color, and the way each vessel reads as a small, self-contained painting in the round.​

Born 1989 in Gifu prefecture, Japan, lives and works in Kyoto, Japan.

baba_yasutaka.name: Baba Yasutaka
baba_yasutaka.web_blurb:
Baba Yasutaka’s meticulously hand-built porcelain sculptures fuse architectural rigor with a luminous sense of light and shadow. The eldest son of a family-run pottery, he completed his training at the Tajimi City Pottery Design and Technical Center in 2017 and quickly gained international attention through exhibitions in Japan, Europe, the US, and Asia. Baba creates intricate “elemental” and “soaring” forms whose faceted, tower-like silhouettes push Hasami’s porcelain tradition into a strikingly contemporary, sculptural language.​

Born 1991 in Hasami, Japan, lives and works in Nagasaki, Japan.

kato_yoshiyasu.name: Kato Yoshiyasu
kato_yoshiyasu.web_blurb:
Kato Yoshiyasu is known for highly refined porcelain vessels that fuse sculptural lightness with everyday function. Trained in craft and design at Kurashiki University of Science and the Arts and in Tajimi, one of Japan’s historic ceramic centers, he works primarily with slip-casting to achieve intricate, “skeletal” forms that appear almost weightless yet remain structurally precise. His practice explores the tension between interior and exterior space, using cutouts, negative space, and crisp white surfaces to create contemplative objects that feel simultaneously industrial and organic.

Born 1985 in Aichi Prefecture, Japan, lives and works in Nishio, Japan.

yuichi_onishi.name: Yuichi Onishi
yuichi_onishi.web_blurb:
Yuichi Onishi’s practice draws from the striking landscape of his hometown of Kumano, composed of dramatic rock formations along the coastline and forested mountains reaching almost to the sea. The impressions these left in his memories, and his personal inner sensations and imagery, are reinterpreted in a continuous process, as he looks for points of connection with the tactile sensations of clay.

Born 1993 in Kumano, Japan, lives and works in Gifu prefecture, Japan.

sota_nakashima.name: Sota Nakashima
sota_nakashima.web_blurb:
Sota Nakashima’s works explore the cycle of life. They are crafted from earth-derived clay, mimicking animal bones, plant seeds, and natural forms to evoke life's beginnings and endings. He sees the formation of clay through geological timescales as a mirror of the much shorter cycles of the living world. Sota’s works try to give the viewer a window into these processes, juxtaposing motifs of decay with the enduring qualities of pottery.

Born in 1996 in Aichi Prefecture, lives and works in Kanazawa, Japan.

eri_gohou.name: Eri Gohou
eri_gohou.web_blurb:
Eri Gohou is a multidisciplinary artist, working with mixed media, ceramics, and performance art. Her overarching theme is “strata”, accumulating layers both metaphorically within the human mind and physically in the deposits of human detritus in the Anthropocene. Her works represent these concepts through the layering of different materials and actions.
Her recent works in the series “Anthropocene Relic 2025: Melted Stratigraphy of the Revolving Vessel” were created in a live performance, shaping the clay on a spinning record as it is used in a live DJ performance. The spinning record evokes the spinning motion of the potter’s wheel, the buddhist prayer wheel and the circle of life. The music is then layered on top of the piece by literally melting it into the clay during the firing process, creating its own Anthropocene strata.

mari_inou.name: Mari Inou
mari_inou.web_blurb:
Mari Inoue graduated from Osaka University of Arts' Craft Department Ceramics Course in 2011 and completed her master's in ceramics there in 2013. She specializes in whimsical animal-themed porcelain and stoneware sculptures, capturing playful narratives and forms in clay.

Born in 1988 in Kobe, Japan.

takuma_watanabe.name: Takuma Watanabe
takuma_watanabe.web_blurb:
Takuma Watanabe works with Bizen clay, an iron-rich, sticky type of clay that has to be fired extremely slowly to prevent cracking. His pieces often feature organic textures from unglazed, high-temperature wood-fired clay, emphasizing wabi-sabi aesthetics with subtle asymmetry and natural ash effects.​​
Takuma creates both functional pieces in the traditional Bizen style, as well as playful sculptural pieces inspired by steampunk aesthetic, replete with gears, bolts, pipes and chimneys.

Born 1968 in Hyogo prefecture, lives and works in Okayama prefecture, Japan.

gentaro_yokoyama.name: Gentaro Yokoyama
gentaro_yokoyama.web_blurb:
Gentaro Yokoyama moved to the U.S. at age 15, discovered ceramics in high school, and studied at the Hartford Art Institute before working at a pottery factory and returning to Japan in 2002. Now based in Tokyo with his gent ceramics studio in Monzennakacho, he creates innovative, neo-pop works using unconventional motifs like amoebas, underwear, and bosozoku-inspired tea bowls that challenge traditional craft boundaries. His pieces have been exhibited at venues like Ginza Mitsukoshi, Art Tower Mito, and internationally, including in the U.S. and South Korea.

Born 1978 in Chiba prefecture, Japan, lives and works in Tokyo, Japan.
